GeoGPT · Guided geology investigation

Combine terrain and shaking to map landslide potential

Where does a fixed model assign higher relative landslide occurrence during the Gorkha earthquake?

The geological task

After an earthquake, teams need a regional picture of where landslides may have occurred. Terrain describes the slopes; the USGS shaking grid describes acceleration. You will supply those numerical maps and an already specified model to GeoGPT, then inspect the calculated relative-occurrence map. The exercise ends with that map and a bounded interpretation.

Your role: inspect the evidence and explain a bounded conclusion. GeoGPT performs the requested analysis. All required settings are already supplied.

Four useful words

Terrain
The shape and height of the ground.

PGA
Peak ground acceleration, the strongest acceleration during shaking.

Relative score
A ranking under this model, not a confirmed landslide or calibrated probability.

Blank map cell
No supplied coverage; it does not mean no hazard.

The idea in plain language

Steeper slopes, local relief and earthquake acceleration describe different parts of the setting in which landslides occur. The supplied empirical equation combines them into a relative score. Empirical means its coefficients were estimated from earlier observations; it is not a calculation of forces resisting a particular slope failure. The same coordinates link the two input tables, so terrain and shaking at each place contribute to that place’s score.

Work in English for a general geology graduate student. This is a fully specified teaching task. Execute the task rather than asking for intended use, validation purpose, thresholds, hypotheses, software, approval or other preferences. Ask only if a named input is missing or unreadable; name it and stop. Do not fabricate execution, observations or citations. Use short plain-language final answers, not JSON or a code dump. End with “Finished. Return to the handout.” Do not append a question or an offer. Read gorkha-terrain.csv, gorkha-shaking.csv and landslide-model.txt. Apply the supplied fixed equation exactly; do not fit, select a threshold or request a landslide inventory. Join cell_id one-to-one and check 6920 matched cells with no duplicates. Preserve PGA in percent g as the equation requires. Execute and save potential-landslides.csv (cell_id,coordinates,score), potential_landslides.py and potential-landslides.png. Plot three vertically stacked maps on a 12 by 16 inch canvas: Terrain; Shaking; Relative occurrence. Same extent, equal spatial aspect, north up; easting/northing in kilometres, at most five ticks per axis; separate readable colorbars. Score scale0..1 labelled “Relative landslide-occurrence score (not calibrated probability)”. Blank cells are missing coverage, not zero score. Inspect the actual plot for overlap. Check any geographic or numeric claim against computed cells. Slope aspect, lithology and groundwater were not provided: do not invent north-facing slopes, landforms or mechanical instability. Final answer only: files, matched-cell count and min/mean/max score, then three short sentences describing the actual map pattern and one plain-language limitation. This is a regional relative-occurrence map, not confirmed failures or a runout map. End here.

3
Minutes 20–32

Read your calculated map

Do this

Open potential-landslides.png under Research Space. Read its score legend. Choose one higher-score area and one lower-score area. Compare the same locations across all three panels.

Why: The fitted equation combines slope, local relief and acceleration. Mean elevation is map context, not one of its predictors. Scores indicate relative modeled tendency, not mechanical factor of safety.

What you should see

Your explanation refers to visible locations and distinguishes high score, confirmed occurrence and missing coverage.

See an example of this checkpoint
Discuss or explore

Can strong shaking alone explain the score pattern? Could the same score arise from different combinations of terrain and shaking?

Minutes 32–45

Finish with a useful map and a limit

Do this

Download the map and its numerical results. In pairs, explain one spatial contrast and one missing kind of evidence. The calculation is finished; spend the remaining time discussing your own observations.

Why: Lithology, material strength, water pressure and runout are not represented. Field or imagery checks would be needed to establish actual landslide locations.

What you should see

You have one map and a short explanation you can defend. No inventory upload, new model fitting or further calculation is required.

Research context and source papers

Rapid earthquake-landslide assessment is an active geoscience application. This exercise illustrates the terrain-plus-shaking calculation with an instructor-fitted model. It does not reproduce the full USGS global model or validate a local probability of failure.

The briefing above supplies what you need during class. These sources are for further study.

  • USGS ground-failure science
  • Nowicki Jessee et al.: global empirical landslide model
  • Gorkha USGS shaking grid
